### `@`  <sub>operator</sub> <a id="op-64"></a>

```
(@) : (b -> c) -> (a -> b) -> a -> c
```

**Composition** — `(f @ g) x` is `f (g x)`.  It reads right to left,
the direction the arrows in its own signature point.

`infixr 9`, the tightest an infix operator gets here, so a chain of
them is one pipeline that every other operator lets group first:
`gain 0.5 @ softClip @ drive 3.0` is a value you can pass around, and
`map (show @ negate) xs` needs no parentheses inside the argument.

This was `compose` and is spelled `@` because the symbol was free and
composition is the one function common enough to earn one.


### `Functor`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Functor f where
```

**What it means to be a container of things you can change.**  `map` is
the method, not a list function — the same reason `++` is `Semigroup`'s
and `>>=` is `Monad`'s.

`signal.ges` adds the `Sig` instance, where the class cannot see it: a
signal is a reactive program's, and this file is in scope for programs
that have none.  What it took is worth stating, because it was the one
instance the fragment had an opinion about — the static fragment
recognises a signal former by *name*, and a method arrives under the
generated `__Functor_Sig_map__`.  `elaborate.resolve_static_methods`
makes that an ordinary global before the fragment reads it, so
`audiograph.FORMERS` lists the generated name beside `mapSig` and a
`map` over a signal is the same node it always was.

### `Zip`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Zip f where
```

**Two containers, combined pointwise.**  `zip f xs ys` applies `f` to
the two element-wise, which at a list stops when the shorter one does
and at a signal is the whole of how two signals meet.

`signal.ges` adds the `Sig` instance, where the class cannot see it —
the same arrangement `Functor` has and for the same reason.  It was
`zipSig` there, which is a name wearing its one type: a signal is
*the* thing you zip in a synth, so the plain word belongs to it as much
as `map` does.

Not `Applicative`.  `<*>` needs `pure` and a partial application per
element, and the audio fragment admits neither; `zip` is the one shape
the engine has a node for, so it is the one the class states.

### `Foldable`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Foldable t where
```

**What a container is, for the purpose of being walked.**  `foldr` is
the one method; `length`, `null`, `sum`, `product`, `all`, `any` and
`elem` below are ordinary functions written against it, and stop being
list functions by saying so.

`foldl` is a method too rather than a derived function: at a list it is
the *accumulating* one and that is a difference in cost, not in result,
which a default written as `foldr` would quietly throw away.

**No `Foldable Score`, deliberately.**  A score could answer "how many
notes" or "how long" and neither is what `length` means; an instance
picking one would be a guess with the authority of a law.  A class with
no instance at a type is a complete answer — unlike `Num`, where a
missing method is a silent placeholder rather than an error.

### `Semigroup`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Semigroup a where
```

`++` is `syntax.md`'s list append — and *music sequence*, and anything
else with an associative join.  So it is a class method rather than a
list function.

**It used to be a plain definition, and that was a bug you could reach.**
`music.ges` declared its own `(++) : [: a :] -> [: a :] -> [: a :]`, and
`prelude.merge` resolves a redefinition by hiding the prelude's — so
inside any program with a `score`, `[1,2] ++ [3]` failed with
`expected 'Score', got 'List'` and list append was unreachable by its own
operator.  `append` still worked, which is why nobody noticed.

The shadow was chosen rather than stumbled into: `music.ges` recorded
that "a class would have left both in scope and clashing", which is true
of adding a class *beside* a plain `(++)` and not of making the plain one
the method.  There is one `++` here and an instance at each type.

### `Monad`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Monad m where
```

**`concat` was `join` all along**, and `music.ges` had written the other
half of the same class: a `(>>=)` over scores, with `Note` for `pure` and
no name for either.  So the monad existed twice, in halves, and was
called neither time.

One class, and `join` rather than `concat` because the operation is not
about lists — flattening a `Maybe (Maybe a)` or a score of scores is the
same fold.  `single` is gone for the same reason: it was `pure` at one
type, and `'x` is already `pure` written as syntax.

### `'`  <sub>operator</sub> <a id="op-39"></a>

```
(') : (Monad m) => a -> m a
```

**`pure`, written as syntax.**  `'60` is one note, `'x` is `[x]` at a
list and `Just x` at a `Maybe` — one element in whatever container the
context asks for.

It was `music.ges`'s and typed `a -> [: a :]`, which is `pure` pinned to
one instance; here it is the method, and `'60 ++ '62` still means a
two-note phrase inside a piece because that is what the surrounding
signature says it is.

**Write the signature.**  `melody : [: Int :]` above the definition is
what settles the container, and without one an ambiguous `'` is not
reported — see `journal.md` Part II.


### `join`

```
join : (Monad m) => m (m a) -> m a
```

One layer off a nested structure — what `concat` was for a list of
lists, and the same function for anything else that nests.


### `Reversible`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Reversible t where
```

**Back to front.**  A class rather than a list function, because the
musical retrograde — a phrase played backwards — *is* this operation and
deserves the word rather than a synonym.  `music.ges` adds the `Score`
instance.

The list one accumulates, so it is linear.  Written the obvious way,
`reverse rest ++ [x]` walks the whole reversed prefix once per element,
which is O(n²) for the one list function nobody expects to be expensive.

### `fstM`

```
fstM : (a, b) ~> a
```

Monotone projections.  `fst`/`snd` above take their argument at the
ordinary arrow, which is Datafun's `□A -> B`, so they cannot be applied
to a *monotone* variable — and that is exactly what `fix` at a product
semilattice binds.  A projection is monotone (a product is ordered
componentwise), so these are the same functions at the arrow that says
so, and they are what makes `fix r => (…, …)` writable.

```

```


### `Prop`  <sub>type alias</sub>

```
type Prop = {()}
```

**The second boolean, and the one a fixed point can use.**  `Prop` is
Datafun's `bool`: `{}` is false, `{()}` is true, `\/` is or, and
`for (u in p) e` is the one-sided conditional.

The difference from `Bool` is that a `Prop` can only *grow* — false to
true and never back — which is what lets a predicate returning one be
computed by `fix`.  `Bool` cannot: `not` runs downhill, and a `fix`
over it need not converge.  Write `Bool` unless you are inside a
fixpoint; `holds` and `guard` convert between them.

An alias rather than a type of its own, because every one of those
properties *is* the set structure and nothing else (`errata.md` D5).


### `Guard`  <sub>class</sub>

```
class Guard a where
```

**What a comprehension's guard clause accepts** — either boolean.

`{e | C, g}` desugars to `for (x in guard g) {e}` with `x` fresh and
unused, so `{x | x in xs, x > 3}` and `{x | x in xs, reaches x}` both
work: at `Prop` `guard` is the identity, at `Bool` it is the injection.
You would rarely write it by hand; it is here because the guard clause
is written in terms of it and an error message may name it.

A class rather than a type-directed desugaring because desugaring runs
long before inference — `errata.md` D5.  The `Bool` instance is
monotone despite the `~>`, and lawfully so: `Bool` is ordered by
equality, and every function out of a discrete type is monotone.


### `Guard Prop`  <sub>instance</sub>

```
instance Guard Prop where
```

### `holds`

```
holds : Prop -> Bool
```

Out of `Prop` and back into `Bool` — "is this one true?", which is how
you read a fixpoint's answer once it has converged.

Takes its argument *discretely* (the plain `->` is `□A -> B`), which is
what makes it non-monotone, as Datafun requires: a growing `Prop` may
not be turned into a `Bool` somewhere still growing.  `empty?` is the
primitive underneath — it cannot be defined, because `for` eliminates
only into a semilattice and `Bool` is not one — and this is the
reading people want.

### `sort`

```
sort : (Ord a) => List a -> List a
```

**Sort, ascending** — a merge sort, because the obvious insertion
is quadratic on exactly the lists somebody bothers to sort.  The
halves come from taking every other element, which needs no length;
the cost is that ties keep no promise about their original order —
said here rather than discovered, since a stable sort would need a
different split and nothing in the tree has asked for one yet.

## Ordering, put to work


### `min`

```
min : (Ord a) => a -> a -> a
```

The smaller of two.


### `max`

```
max : (Ord a) => a -> a -> a
```

The larger of two.


### `clamp`

```
clamp : (Ord a) => a -> a -> a -> a
```

`clamp lo hi x` — `x`, held between the two.

Used at every boundary where a number arrives from outside: a knob is
the one value a synth does not compute, the offline renderer drives
every control channel with the *sample index*, and an unclamped filter
coefficient leaves 0..1 within a few hundred samples and diverges
(`twoknobs.ges` says so at length).  A pointer is the same kind of
outside.


## Blending


### `mix`

```
mix : (Num a) => a -> a -> a -> a
```

`mix a b t` — linear interpolation: at `t` of 0 the first, at 1 the
second.


### `bimix`

```
bimix : (Num a, Floating a) => a -> a -> a -> a
```

`bimix a b t` — the same, driven by a **bipolar** `t`: −1 is the first,
0 is halfway, 1 is the second.

What an oscillator hands you is −1..1, so this is the blend a modulation
actually wants — `bimix dark bright (sine 5.0)` sweeps between two
colours, two cutoffs or two pictures without a conversion at the call.

Spelled out rather than written `mix a b (unipolar t)`, which is what it
means: `unipolar` is a signal function in `synth.ges` — a `map` — and
the prelude comes before there are signals.  The arithmetic is three
characters and the dependency would be a layer.

**Two constraints where `mix` has one, and the half is why.**  `mix`
names no literal, so `Num` carries it at every numeric type including
`Sig Int`; this one has to halve, and a fractional literal is
`Floating`.  Both are needed and neither implies the other — they are
synthetic classes `declarations.py` generates rather than a hierarchy a
program could write, so there is no superclass to inherit `+` from.

It costs nothing real: the types with a meaningful midpoint are exactly
the types that have one.


## Floats


### `toFloat`

```
toFloat : Int -> Float
```


### `floor`

```
floor : Float -> Int
```

The greatest integer not above its argument — floor, not truncation,
so it agrees with `prim_div_int` on negatives.


### `ceil`

```
ceil : Float -> Int
```

The least integer not below its argument — `floor` the other way.

Not a primitive: `ceil x` is `negate (floor (negate x))` exactly, at
every float including the integral ones, so a sixth primitive to keep
in agreement with the interpreter would buy nothing.  Same argument as
`tan` and `pow`.


### `sin`

```
sin : Float -> Float
```

The transcendentals.  Each is libm's function of the same name, on both
sides of the audio pipeline: the interpreter calls Python's `math`, and
generated code calls `llvm.<name>.f64`, and the two are the same libm on
the same machine.  `spec/liveaudio.md` open question 2 argues why that
identity is what matters and `test/test_transcendental.py` measures it —
these are not correctly-rounded functions, so nothing *but* being the
same implementation would make the comparison exact.

The angle is in radians.


### `cos`

```
cos : Float -> Float
```


### `sqrt`

```
sqrt : Float -> Float
```

Undefined below zero — the interpreter raises where C returns NaN, so
this is an error rather than a value the two would disagree about.


### `exp`

```
exp : Float -> Float
```


### `log`

```
log : Float -> Float
```

Natural log.  Undefined at and below zero, for the reason `sqrt` gives.


### `tan`

```
tan : Float -> Float
```

Not a primitive, and it does not need to be: written here it is the same
expression on both sides, so it is bit-identical by construction rather
than by libm agreeing about `tan`.  (Which is also why `llvm.tan.f64`
needing LLVM 19 costs nothing.)


### `pow`

```
pow : Float -> Float -> Float
```

`pow b e` is `b ** e`, for a positive base.  Same argument as `tan`: an
identity in the language beats a sixth primitive to keep in agreement.

### Envelopes


#### `append`

```
append : List a -> List a -> List a
```

`++` at a list, which is the only thing that calls it.  Here rather
than above because `++` *is* its public face: `instance Semigroup
(List b)` is one line long and this is that line's body.


#### `everyOther`

```

```

Every second element: the evens of a list and the evens of its tail
are its two halves, interleaved.

#### `reverseOnto`

```
reverseOnto : List a -> List a -> List a
```

`reverseOnto xs acc` is `reverse xs ++ acc` without building the
intermediate — the accumulator that makes `reverse` linear.  Written
the obvious way, `reverse` walks the reversed prefix once per element,
which is O(n²) for the one list function nobody expects to be
expensive.
